patient.chief_complaint: New bilateral ptosis and diplopia in a patient on chemotherapy for lymphoma
patient.history_present_illness: A 57-year-old man with high-grade peripheral T-cell lymphoma receiving EPOCH chemotherapy (after 4 of 6 planned cycles) presented with new bilateral ptosis and diplopia over 5 weeks. He had been doing well on chemotherapy with near-complete metabolic response on interim PET-CT, but his oncology team noted new drooping of his left eyelid at a clinic visit. The patient confirmed the ptosis had been present for 5 weeks and was progressive. He developed horizontal diplopia 3 weeks ago, initially intermittent and worse after a long day, and now present during most of his waking hours. He also reported jaw fatigue when eating — he rested between bites during meal times. His voice had become increasingly nasal, a change his wife noted clearly. He denied significant dysphagia. He had been attributing all new neurological symptoms to chemotherapy toxicity, which had already caused peripheral neuropathy from vincristine. He had multiple prior episodes of febrile neutropenia requiring hospitalization and had a severe sepsis episode after his second cycle requiring one week in the ICU. His oncologist was concerned about: (1) central nervous system lymphoma invasion, (2) paraneoplastic syndrome, (3) chemotherapy neurotoxicity (vincristine-induced cranial neuropathy), and (4) opportunistic infection. Brain MRI was performed and reported as showing no CNS lymphoma. He was referred to neurology for NMJ evaluation after the oncologist noted the fatigable pattern was inconsistent with typical vincristine neuropathy, which causes peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy rather than cranial neuropathy with fatigability.

results.title: Paraneoplastic NMJ disorders in lymphoma
results.finding: MG has been reported in association with non-Hodgkin lymphoma including PTCL; anti-AChR antibodies can be paraneoplastic; treatment of underlying lymphoma may improve MG; concurrent vincristine neuropathy can complicate clinical picture

results.title: Anti-titin antibodies and thymoma vs paraneoplastic MG
results.finding: Anti-titin positive in MG can indicate thymoma OR paraneoplastic MG from other malignancies; CT chest should be performed but anti-titin alone does not confirm thymoma when CT is negative

output.summary: Paraneoplastic MG with anti-AChR antibodies has been reported in T-cell lymphoma and other non-SCLC malignancies. Anti-titin positive without CT-confirmed thymoma in a lymphoma patient is consistent with paraneoplastic mechanism. IVIG and pyridostigmine are appropriate; corticosteroids are problematic given lymphoma treatment. Lymphoma treatment remains priority.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), paraneoplastic in context of peripheral T-cell lymphoma; concurrent vincristine peripheral neuropathy

differential.key_features: Vincristine causes sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy, not cranial neuropathy with fatigability; NCS shows axonal sensorimotor neuropathy from vincristine but this cannot explain fatigable ptosis and jaw fatigue; AChR antibodies confirm MG
Anti-VGCC negative; high-rate RNS shows only 12% increment (not >100%); ocular symptoms prominent (LEMS usually spares ocular); MG confirmed
MRI brain and spine: no CNS lymphoma; no leptomeningeal enhancement; no cranial nerve enhancement; MG is the diagnosis
ICU stay was 6 cycles ago (cycle 2); patient has recovered; no fibrillation potentials on needle EMG; AChR antibodies confirm NMJ disorder not myopathy

critical_actions: MRI brain/spine to exclude CNS lymphoma before attributing neurological symptoms to MG
High-rate RNS (30-40 Hz) to exclude LEMS — critical differential in cancer patient
Anti-VGCC testing to definitively exclude LEMS
SFEMG when RNS is borderline (as in this case)
IVIG preferred over corticosteroids for MG in active lymphoma (steroids are already part of EPOCH regimen)
Monitor vincristine neuropathy and MG separately — both contribute to weakness
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT attribute all neurological symptoms to vincristine toxicity without NMJ evaluation
Do NOT start additional high-dose corticosteroids for MG without oncology co-management (steroids in active lymphoma)
Do NOT delay pyridostigmine waiting for all tests — symptomatic treatment can start while workup continues
Do NOT use aminoglycosides in this or any MG patient
key_reasoning_points: Fatigable ptosis and jaw fatigue in a chemotherapy patient require systematic NMJ evaluation — vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy but NOT fatigable cranial nerve involvement
High-rate RNS (30-40 Hz) is crucial in cancer patients to distinguish MG (post-synaptic) from LEMS (pre-synaptic paraneoplastic) — no >100% increment confirms MG not LEMS
Anti-titin positive without CT thymoma in lymphoma patient suggests paraneoplastic MG — lymphoma is the cancer driving autoimmune NMJ disorder
IVIG is the preferred treatment for MG in active lymphoma — avoids additional immunosuppression conflicts with oncology treatment
CNS lymphoma must always be excluded first in lymphoma patients with new neurological symptoms — MRI required before attributing to peripheral NMJ disorder

red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician attributes ALL neurological symptoms to vincristine toxicity, missing concurrent MG diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Vincristine causes axonal sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy (confirmed by NCS); it does NOT cause fatigable cranial nerve involvement or jaw fatigue; SFEMG and AChR antibodies identify concurrent MG
